Monopoly. A market structure in which a single firm is the sole supplier of a good with no close substitutes. Unlike perfectly competitive markets where many firms take the market price as given, a monopolist is a price maker. It chooses the price-quantity combination that maximizes profit, knowing that lowering price increases quantity demanded and vice versa.

Monopolies arise from barriers to entry that prevent competitors from entering. These barriers can be legal like patents and licenses, technological like economies of scale, or network-based when switching costs are high. These barriers allow the monopolist to sustain above-normal profits indefinitely.

The monopolist faces the market demand curve and sets quantity and price to maximize profit. Competitive firms instead set quantity and take price as given. A monopolist produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and sets price on the demand curve above that quantity. This results in higher price and lower quantity compared to perfect competition. Consumer surplus shrinks—some converts to monopolist profit, and some is lost as deadweight loss or allocative inefficiency.

Monopoly power comes from several sources. Patents give pharmaceutical firms monopolies on drugs for twenty years. Economies of scale create natural monopolies in utilities and rail. A single firm can serve the market at lower per-unit cost than multiple competitors. Network effects make social media platforms more valuable as membership grows, creating winner-take-all dynamics. Licensing and regulation grant exclusive rights like broadcast licenses and utility franchises.

Governments respond to monopoly through antitrust law. They may block mergers, break up monopolies, or regulate pricing to protect consumer welfare. Price regulation can reduce monopoly profit but may reduce output if set too low or do little if set above what the monopolist would charge anyway.

Monopoly power is central to debates over fairness and the role of government in markets. The fear of monopoly motivated U.S. antitrust law and continues to animate scrutiny of tech giants. Yet monopolies aren't inherently evil. Patents reward innovation. Natural monopolies may be more efficient than multiple competing firms. The real economic harm comes from productive inefficiency—monopolists don't minimize costs—and allocative inefficiency. They produce too little at too high a price. Understanding monopoly versus competition is foundational to understanding why some markets are regulated.
